# Managing jobs
Source: https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/managing-jobs

Estimate what a job will cost, label and track it, read its cost and timing, see what ran on the device, and reconnect to it later.

<Info>
  API Reference:
  [qbraid.runtime.native](https://qbraid.github.io/qBraid/stubs/qbraid.runtime.native.html)
</Info>

Everything on this page works the same on every device you reach through `QbraidProvider`, whichever vendor or [submission path](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/getting-started#submission-paths) it uses. The examples use the free QIR simulator, `qbraid:qbraid:sim:qir-sv`:

```python
from qbraid.runtime import QbraidProvider

provider = QbraidProvider()
device = provider.get_device("qbraid:qbraid:sim:qir-sv")

bell = """
OPENQASM 3.0;
include "stdgates.inc";
qubit[2] q;
bit[2] c;
h q[0];
cx q[0], q[1];
c = measure q;
"""
```

## Before you submit

### Check the device

```python
device.status()
# <DeviceStatus.ONLINE: 'ONLINE'>

device.queue_depth()
# 0
```

`device.run()` warns when a device isn't `ONLINE`: the job may be refused, or wait a long time. `provider.get_devices()` lists the devices you can submit to now. Pass `include_retired=True` to also list devices that have been retired.

### Estimate the cost

`provider.client.estimate_cost` prices a job before you submit it, in qBraid credits:

```python
estimate = provider.client.estimate_cost("aws:iqm:qpu:garnet", shots=100)

estimate.pricingAvailable
# True
estimate.estimatedCost
# Credits('44.5')
```

Some devices are priced dynamically by their vendor, so no estimate is possible in advance. For those, `pricingAvailable` is `False` and `reason` says why, such as `'dynamic_pricing_unavailable'`. Devices with `openquantum:` IDs estimate `0`, because they spend credits from your linked [Open Quantum](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/open-quantum) account rather than qBraid credits.

The [device catalog](https://account.qbraid.com/devices) shows the same prices.

### Check your balance

```python
balance = provider.client.get_credits_balance()
balance["qbraidCredits"]
```

The balance belongs to the organization your API key is tied to.

## Submitting

```python
job = device.run(
    bell,
    shots=100,
    name="bell-test",
    tags={"experiment": "docs-managing-jobs"},
)
job.id
# 'qbraid:qbraid:sim:qir-sv-8ce1-qjob-6ad8144c34188ba734e7a279'
```

| Argument          | Effect                                                                                              |
| :---------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `shots`           | Number of shots.                                                                                    |
| `name`            | A name for the job, shown in [Quantum Jobs](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/account/quantum-jobs).                              |
| `tags`            | Key-value labels, with string, integer or boolean values. [Find jobs by tag](#find-past-jobs) later. |
| `runtime_options` | Options passed to the device. See [Runtime options](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/getting-started#runtime-options). |

Keep `job.id`: it is all you need to [get the job back](#reconnect-to-a-job) later.

To run several circuits at once, see [Batch & group jobs](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/jobs).

## While it runs

```python
job.status()
# <QUEUED: 'job is queued'>

job.queue_position()
# 3
```

`queue_position()` returns `None` once the job has left the queue, or when the device doesn't report positions.

A job moves through `INITIALIZING`, `QUEUED`, `RUNNING`, and then one of `COMPLETED`, `FAILED` or `CANCELLED`. `job.is_terminal_state()` tells you whether it has finished.

### Wait for it

`job.result()` blocks until the job finishes. Pass `timeout`, in seconds, to give up waiting. The job keeps running.

```python
result = job.result(timeout=600)
```

`job.wait_for_final_state(timeout=600, poll_interval=5)` waits without fetching the result. In async code, `await job.async_result()` waits without blocking the event loop.

### Cancel it

```python
job.cancel()
```

`cancel()` raises `JobStateError` if the job has already finished. A job that has started running on a QPU may finish before the cancellation reaches it.

## Results

```python
result.success
# True

result.data.get_counts()
# {'00': 46, '11': 54}
```

`result.data` also has `get_probabilities()`, and `measurements` for the individual shots where the device returns them.

### Cost and timing

`result.details` records what the job actually cost and how long it took:

```python
result.details["cost"]
# Credits('0')

result.details["time_stamps"]
# TimeStamps(createdAt=datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 21, 1, 24, 30, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc),
#            endedAt=datetime.datetime(2026, 10, 21, 1, 24, 30, tzinfo=datetime.timezone.utc),
#            executionDuration=12)
```

`executionDuration` is in milliseconds.

### When a job fails

A job that doesn't complete still returns a result, with `success` set to `False` and no data. When the platform gives a reason, it is in `details["status_message"]`:

```python
result = job.result()

if not result.success:
    print(result.details["status"])
    print(result.details.get("status_message"))
```

## After it runs

### What you submitted

`job.program()` returns the program as qBraid received it, after any conversion from your framework:

```python
job.program()
# Program(format='qasm3', data='OPENQASM 3.0;\ninclude "stdgates.inc";\nqubit[2] q; ...')
```

### What ran on the device

`job.compiled_program()` returns the program the device's compiler produced. On a QPU this shows which physical qubits your circuit ran on and the native gates it was compiled to, which the counts alone can't tell you:

```python
compiled = job.compiled_program()
compiled.format
# 'qir.ll'
```

| Devices                                                                                      | Format   |
| :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------- |
| [IQM through Amazon Braket](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/aws#retrieving-the-compiled-program)               | `qasm3`  |
| [Rigetti](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/rigetti#the-compiled-program), direct or through Amazon Braket              | `quil`   |
| [QIR simulator](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/getting-started#basic-usage)                     | `qir.ll` |

It returns `None` when there is no compiled program: the job hasn't finished, the device doesn't report one, or the job predates this feature. A batch job returns a list, one program per circuit.

### Reconnect to a job

A job ID is enough to get a job back, for example after restarting a notebook kernel, or on another machine:

```python
from qbraid.runtime import load_job

job = load_job("qbraid:qbraid:sim:qir-sv-8ce1-qjob-6ad8144c34188ba734e7a279", provider="qbraid")
job.status()
# <COMPLETED: 'job has successfully run'>
```

The returned job supports everything on this page.

### Find past jobs

`provider.client.list_jobs` searches your jobs. Filter by tag, status or text:

```python
jobs = provider.client.list_jobs(tags={"experiment": "docs-managing-jobs"})
[(j.jobQrn, j.name, j.status) for j in jobs]
# [('qbraid:qbraid:sim:qir-sv-8ce1-qjob-6ad8144c34188ba734e7a279', 'bell-test', <COMPLETED: ...>)]
```

| Filter         | Example                                                    |
| :------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------- |
| `tags`         | `{"experiment": "bell-state"}`                             |
| `status`       | `"COMPLETED"`, `"FAILED"`                                  |
| `status_group` | `"pending"` (not finished yet), `"returned"` (finished), `"all"` |
| `search`       | Text matched against your jobs                             |
| `page`, `limit` | Pagination                                                |

Pass a result's `jobQrn` to `load_job` to work with that job. [Quantum Jobs](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/account/quantum-jobs) shows the same jobs in your account.

# Batch and group jobs
Source: https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/jobs

Run several circuits through the QbraidProvider as separate jobs, as one batch job on one device, or as a group of jobs across devices.

<Info>
  API Reference:
  [qbraid.runtime.native](https://qbraid.github.io/qBraid/stubs/qbraid.runtime.native.html)
</Info>

There are three ways to run more than one circuit through the `QbraidProvider`. For a single
circuit, see [Run on qBraid](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/getting-started#basic-usage).

## Which one to use

|                       | Separate jobs                      | Batch job                                       | Group job                            |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| **Scope**             | Multiple circuits, one device      | Multiple circuits, one device                   | Multiple jobs, any devices           |
| **Submission**        | `device.run(programs)`             | `device.run(programs, as_batch=True)`           | `GroupJobSession` context            |
| **Return type**       | A list of `QbraidJob`              | Single `QbraidJob` → `BatchResult`              | Multiple `QbraidJob` → `GroupResult` |
| **Use case**          | A few unrelated circuits           | Parameterized circuits, algorithm variants      | Cross-device benchmarks, sweeps      |
| **Supported devices** | All devices                        | Devices with `device.profile.batch_job_support` | All devices                          |

## Separate jobs

Passing a list of programs to `device.run()` submits each one as its own job:

```python
programs = [bell_circuit, ghz_circuit, qft_circuit]
jobs = device.run(programs, shots=100)
results = [job.result() for job in jobs]
```

For async applications, [`async_result()`](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/overview#async-results) awaits a
job without blocking the event loop:

```python
result = await job.async_result(timeout=120, poll_interval=5)
print(result.data.get_counts())
```

## Batch Jobs

Submit multiple circuits as a **single job** to a device that supports batched execution.
Unlike [group jobs](#group-jobs), which coordinate independent jobs across devices, batch
jobs send all circuits in one request and return a unified result.

### Submitting a Batch

Pass a list of programs with `as_batch=True` to submit them as a single job:

```python
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qbraid.runtime import QbraidProvider

provider = QbraidProvider()
device = provider.get_device("qbraid:equal1:sim:bell-1")

# Define multiple circuits
bell = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
bell.h(0)
bell.cx(0, 1)
bell.measure([0, 1], [0, 1])

ghz = QuantumCircuit(3, 3)
ghz.h(0)
ghz.cx(0, 1)
ghz.cx(1, 2)
ghz.measure([0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 2])

x_gate = QuantumCircuit(1, 1)
x_gate.x(0)
x_gate.measure(0, 0)

# Submit all three circuits as a single batch job
job = device.run([bell, ghz, x_gate], shots=1000, as_batch=True)
print(type(job))
# <class 'qbraid.runtime.native.job.QbraidJob'>
```

A batch submission returns a single `QbraidJob`, not a list. All circuits share the same
job ID, device, and shot count.

<Note>
  `as_batch=True` requires a device that supports batch execution. You can check
  this via the device profile's `batch_job_support` flag. Passing
  `as_batch=True` to an unsupported device raises a `ValueError`. Devices that
  support it include `qbraid:equal1:sim:bell-1`, the QUDORA simulators
  `qudora:qudora:sim:qvls-q1-emulator` and `qudora:qudora:sim:qamelion`, and the
  [GPU simulators](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/gpu-simulators#batch-jobs)
  `qbraid:qbraid:sim:gpu-sv` and `qbraid:qbraid:sim:gpu-tn`.
</Note>

### Retrieving Batch Results

Calling `job.result()` on a batch job returns a `BatchResult` object:

<CodeGroup>

```python Retrieval
result = job.result()
print(type(result))
print(result.num_circuits)
```

```text Output
<class 'qbraid.runtime.result.BatchResult'>
3
```

</CodeGroup>

`BatchResult` provides two ways to access measurement data:

**Aggregate access** — indexed by circuit position:

<CodeGroup>

```python Aggregate
# All circuit counts as a list
all_counts = result.data.get_counts()
for i, counts in enumerate(all_counts):
    print(f"Circuit {i}: {counts}")
```

```text Output
Circuit 0: {'00': 512, '11': 488}
Circuit 1: {'000': 498, '111': 502}
Circuit 2: {'1': 1000}
```

</CodeGroup>

**Per-circuit access** — each circuit's `Result` is a full object with its own status and metadata:

<CodeGroup>

```python Per-Circuit
for i, circuit_result in enumerate(result.results):
    print(f"Circuit {i}: status={circuit_result.success}, counts={circuit_result.data.get_counts()}")
```

```text Output
Circuit 0: status=True, counts={'00': 512, '11': 488}
Circuit 1: status=True, counts={'000': 498, '111': 502}
Circuit 2: status=True, counts={'1': 1000}
```

</CodeGroup>

### BatchResult Properties

| Property       | Type           | Description                                                             |
| -------------- | -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `num_circuits` | `int`          | Number of circuits in the batch                                         |
| `results`      | `list[Result]` | Per-circuit `Result` objects                                            |
| `data`         | `ResultData`   | Aggregated data — `get_counts()` and `get_probabilities()` return lists |
| `details`      | `list[dict]`   | Per-circuit metadata (e.g. `compiledOutput`)                            |
| `success`      | `bool`         | Whether the overall job completed successfully                          |
| `device_id`    | `str`          | Device QRN                                                              |
| `job_id`       | `str`          | Job QRN                                                                 |

### Per-Circuit Error Handling

In a batch job, individual circuits can fail while others succeed. Failed circuits
carry their own error message, accessible through their per-circuit result:

```python
result = job.result()

for i, circuit_result in enumerate(result.results):
    if not circuit_result.success:
        print(f"Circuit {i} failed: {circuit_result.details.get('statusMsg')}")
    else:
        print(f"Circuit {i}: {circuit_result.data.get_counts()}")
```

## Group Jobs

### Why Group?

When running related quantum experiments — parameter sweeps, algorithm comparisons,
cross-device benchmarks — you often end up with many independent jobs that are logically
part of the same workflow. Without grouping, these jobs are scattered across your job history
with no way to track or retrieve them together.

**`GroupJobSession`** solves this by grouping any number of jobs under a single group ID.
Key benefits:

- **Cross-device, cross-provider**: submit jobs to different backends (AWS SV1, IonQ, qBraid simulators) within the same group
- **Unified tracking**: all jobs share a group QRN visible in the qBraid dashboard
- **Aggregated results**: retrieve all results at once with `group.results()`
- **Lifecycle management**: auto-close with TTL, cancellation, completion callbacks

<Note>
  `GroupJobSession` builds its own API client rather than borrowing one from a provider. The examples below rely on credentials already configured on the machine, through `qbraid configure` or the `QBRAID_API_KEY` environment variable.

  If you pass your key in code instead, hand the session your provider's client. Without it the session cannot see your credentials and fails to authenticate:

  ```python
  provider = QbraidProvider(api_key=API_KEY)
  
  with GroupJobSession(name="sweep", client=provider.client) as group:
      job = device.run(circuit, shots=100)
  ```
</Note>

### Context Manager

The simplest way to use group jobs. All jobs submitted inside the `with` block are
automatically tagged with the group ID. The group closes when the block exits.

```python
from qbraid.runtime import GroupJobSession, QbraidProvider

provider = QbraidProvider()

bell = """
OPENQASM 3.0;
include "stdgates.inc";
qubit[2] q;
bit[2] c;
h q[0];
cx q[0], q[1];
c = measure q;
"""

# All jobs inside this block belong to the same group
with GroupJobSession(name="Bell State Sweep") as group:
    # Submit to different devices within the same group
    sv1 = provider.get_device("aws:aws:sim:sv1")
    job1 = sv1.run(bell, shots=100)

    tn1 = provider.get_device("aws:aws:sim:tn1")
    job2 = tn1.run(bell, shots=100)

    print(f"Group ID: {group.group_id}")
    print(f"Jobs in group: {len(group.jobs)}")

# Group ID: group:abc-123456
# Jobs in group: 2
```

### Manual Open / Close

For interactive workflows like Jupyter notebooks, you can open and close the group
manually across multiple cells.

```python
from qbraid.runtime import GroupJobSession, QbraidProvider

provider = QbraidProvider()

# Create and open the group manually
group = GroupJobSession(name="Notebook Experiment")
group.open()

# Cell 2: submit jobs (can be in separate notebook cells)
device = provider.get_device("qbraid:qbraid:sim:qir-sv")
job1 = device.run(circuit_1, shots=100)
job2 = device.run(circuit_2, shots=100)

# Cell 3: close when done submitting
group.close()
```

### Auto-Close with TTL

Set a time-to-live so the group automatically closes after a duration, even if you
forget to call `close()` or your kernel crashes. Defaults to 1 hour (3600s) if not specified.

```python
# Group auto-closes after 60 seconds (default: 3600s / 1 hour)
with GroupJobSession(name="Quick Sweep", max_ttl=60) as group:
    device = provider.get_device("aws:aws:sim:sv1")
    job = device.run(bell, shots=10)
    print(f"TTL: {group.max_ttl}s")
```

<Tip>
  The `max_ttl` parameter accepts values from 1 to 86400 seconds (24 hours). If
  not specified, the backend defaults to 3600 seconds (1 hour).
</Tip>

### Retrieving Results

After closing a group, retrieve all job results at once. `group.results()` blocks until
every job reaches a terminal state (completed, failed, or cancelled).

<CodeGroup>

```python Submission
with GroupJobSession(name="Result Demo") as group:
    device = provider.get_device("qbraid:qbraid:sim:qir-sv")
    job1 = device.run(bell, shots=100)
    job2 = device.run(bell, shots=100)

# Wait for all jobs and collect results
results = group.results(timeout=300)
print(results)

for job_id, result in results.results.items():
    print(f"{job_id}: {result.data.get_counts()}")
```

```text Results
GroupResult(group_id='group:ghi-345678', total=2, successful=2, failed=0)
job:aaa-111: {'00': 48, '11': 52}
job:bbb-222: {'00': 51, '11': 49}
```

</CodeGroup>

You can also filter results by outcome:

```python
# Only successful results
successful = results.successful()

# Only failed results
failed = results.failed()
```

### Completion Callback

Register a callback that fires automatically when all jobs complete. The callback
runs at context exit, after the group is closed.

<CodeGroup>

```python Callback Setup
def analyze(results):
    """Process results when all jobs finish."""
    for job_id, result in results.items():
        counts = result.data.get_counts()
        print(f"{job_id}: {counts}")

with GroupJobSession(name="With Callback") as group:
    device = provider.get_device("qbraid:qbraid:sim:qir-sv")
    device.run(bell, shots=100)
    device.run(bell, shots=100)

    # Callback fires automatically when the context exits
    group.on_all_complete(analyze, timeout=600)
```

```text Callback Output
job:ccc-333: {'00': 47, '11': 53}
job:ddd-444: {'00': 50, '11': 50}
```

</CodeGroup>

### Cancellation

Cancel a group and all its non-terminal jobs:

```python
group = GroupJobSession(name="Cancellable")
group.open()

device = provider.get_device("aws:aws:sim:sv1")
job1 = device.run(bell, shots=1000)
job2 = device.run(bell, shots=1000)

# Cancel the entire group and reset the session
group.cancel()

print(group.status())
# GroupStatus.CANCELLED
```


# Device calibrations and connectivity
Source: https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/calibrations

Fetch live coupling maps and calibration data for QPUs on qBraid, plot connectivity graphs, and use the data to place circuits on the best-calibrated qubits before submitting.

<Info>
  Calibration data is refreshed from each hardware provider roughly hourly.
</Info>

Superconducting QPUs are not uniform: qubits differ in readout fidelity, and
two-qubit gates only exist between physically coupled pairs, each with its own
error rate. The [QbraidProvider](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/getting-started) exposes
both facts programmatically, so you can inspect a device before you submit to
it, and place your circuit on the qubits where it will perform best.

## Do you need this?

No. Calibration-aware qubit selection is an optimization, not a prerequisite —
you can submit jobs without ever calling `get_calibrations()`. When you submit a
circuit, the provider's compiler already chooses a physical layout for you,
using these same calibration tables to avoid the worst qubits.

Reach for this page when you hit a question the default path does not answer:

- **"Why did my results change since last week?"** Devices drift and are
  recalibrated continuously, so comparing snapshots often explains it.
- **"Which device should I run on?"** Qubit count alone says little; error rates
  and coherence times say more.
- **"Can I beat the default layout?"** For deep circuits, pinning a
  high-fidelity qubit chain can outperform automatic placement.
- **Noise characterization and benchmarking**, where the calibration data is
  itself the object of study.

## Fetching calibration data

Every `QbraidDevice` has two entry points:

```python
from qbraid.runtime import QbraidProvider

provider = QbraidProvider()
device = provider.get_device("rigetti:rigetti:qpu:cepheus-1-108q")

device.coupling_map
# ((0, 1), (0, 9), (1, 2), (1, 10), (2, 3), ...)  193 physical qubit pairs

calibration = device.get_calibrations()
calibration.last_calibrated
# '2026-07-21T20:05:45+00:00'
```

`coupling_map` is the device's physical connectivity: sorted, deduplicated
`(source, target)` qubit pairs, derived from the calibrated two-qubit gate
edges. It is cached on the device instance, since hardware topology does not
change between calibrations.

`get_calibrations()` returns the full live snapshot and always fetches fresh
data. The two most useful fields:

```python
# Per-edge two-qubit gate error, keyed by gate name
calibration.edges["gateError"]["cz"][0]
# EdgeEntry(source=0, target=1, value=0.0246)

# Per-qubit metrics
calibration.qubits["0"]
# QubitCalibration(readout_error=0.04, gate_error={'rb': 0.0019}, ...)
```

Both return `None` for devices without published calibration data, such as
simulators.

### Devices with calibration data

| Physical device        | Qubits | Edges | Example device IDs                                                     |
| ---------------------- | ------ | ----- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Rigetti Cepheus-1-108Q | 107    | 193   | `rigetti:rigetti:qpu:cepheus-1-108q`, `aws:rigetti:qpu:cepheus-1-108q` |
| IQM Garnet             | 20     | 30    | `aws:iqm:qpu:garnet`                                                   |
| IQM Emerald            | 54     | 85    | `aws:iqm:qpu:emerald`                                                  |
| AQT Ibex-Q1            | 12     | 0     | `aws:aqt:qpu:ibex-q1`                                                  |

<Note>
  All device IDs that map to the same physical hardware share one calibration
  snapshot, so `rigetti:rigetti:qpu:cepheus-1-108q` and
  `aws:rigetti:qpu:cepheus-1-108q` return identical data.
</Note>

<Note>
  A device can have calibration data with an empty edge list. AQT's Ibex-Q1 is a
  trapped-ion system with all-to-all connectivity, so there are no discrete
  coupling edges to report: `coupling_map` returns an empty tuple, not `None`.
  For IonQ trapped-ion devices, see `device.profile.characterization` instead.
</Note>

You can also query the underlying REST endpoint directly, which works for any
device ID including those not available for direct submission:

```bash
curl -H "X-API-Key: $QBRAID_API_KEY" \
  https://api.qbraid.com/api/v1/devices/rigetti:rigetti:qpu:cepheus-1-108q/calibrations
```

## Plotting the connectivity graph

The `qbraid.visualization` module renders the graph in one call, colored by
live calibration data. Edges are colored by two-qubit gate error and nodes by
readout error, on a single-hue scale where darker is better, matching the
topology view in qBraid Lab:

```python
from qbraid.visualization import plot_connectivity_graph

plot_connectivity_graph(device)
```

<div
  style={{ display: "flex", justifyContent: "center", alignItems: "center" }}
>
  <img src="/v2/sdk/_static/cepheus-connectivity.png" width="75%"></img>
</div>

The dotted outline is a qubit in the lattice footprint with no working
couplings. Light qubits and edges are the ones to avoid.

The layout comes from the device document's `topology` config, so square
lattices (Rigetti) and clipped lattices (IQM) both render their true physical
geometry; devices without a lattice config fall back to a force-directed
layout. To build a custom plot, the `lattice_positions` helper maps qubit ids
to grid coordinates from the same config:

```python
from qbraid.visualization import lattice_positions

topology = device.client.get_device(device.id).topology
# {'type': 'square-lattice', 'rows': 12, 'cols': 9}

positions = lattice_positions(topology, range(108))
# {0: (0, 0), 1: (1, 0), ..., 107: (8, -11)}
```

The same call works unchanged on any device with calibration data. IQM's
Garnet renders its clipped diamond lattice:

```python
garnet = provider.get_device("aws:iqm:qpu:garnet")
plot_connectivity_graph(garnet)
```

<div
  style={{ display: "flex", justifyContent: "center", alignItems: "center" }}
>
  <img src="/v2/sdk/_static/garnet-connectivity.png" width="60%"></img>
</div>

## Choosing the best qubits

With the calibration data in hand, qubit selection becomes a graph problem,
and `best_qubits` solves it in one call:

```python
device.best_qubits(2)
# (81, 82)                -- best-calibrated pair, 2026-07-24 snapshot

device.best_qubits(5)
# (91, 82, 81, 90, 99)    -- connected chain, in path order
```

`best_qubits(n)` fetches a fresh calibration snapshot and returns the
connected chain of `n` physical qubits maximizing estimated fidelity: the
product of `(1 - error)` over each qubit's readout and single-qubit gate
errors and each edge's two-qubit gate error. Folding readout in matters:
readout error varies by an order of magnitude across the lattice, and the
edge with the lowest two-qubit error regularly sits on a qubit that reads out
poorly. See [Scoring
edges](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/rigetti#scoring-edges) for a
hardware-verified example where the two rankings disagree.

A few variations:

```python
device.best_qubits(2, gate="cz")   # restrict edge errors to one gate
device.best_qubits(1)              # best single qubit (e.g. for a T1 sweep)
```

By default each edge uses its best calibrated two-qubit gate; naming a gate
with no calibrated edges raises `ValueError` and lists the ones available.
Devices with qubit metrics but no coupling edges (all-to-all connectivity, such
as AQT's Ibex-Q1) return the `n` individually best qubits. Devices without
calibration data return `None`. Asking for a longer connected chain than the
coupling graph contains raises `ValueError`, as does asking an all-to-all device
for more qubits than it has calibrated, or calling `best_qubits` on an analog
device, which has no fixed qubit lattice to choose from.

Metrics a device does not publish are skipped rather than penalized, so a qubit
is never scored down for data its provider withholds. Ibex-Q1 publishes no
readout error at all, for instance, so its ranking rests on single-qubit gate
error alone.

The chain search is exhaustive, and its cost climbs steeply once `n` approaches
device scale: on Cepheus-1-108Q (107 qubits, 193 edges) `best_qubits(20)`
returns in about a second and `best_qubits(24)` in under ten, while
`best_qubits(30)` does not finish in a minute. Practical circuit widths are
well inside that; whole-device chains are not what this is for.

<div
  style={{ display: "flex", justifyContent: "center", alignItems: "center" }}
>
  <img src="/v2/sdk/_static/cepheus-best-chain.png" width="75%"></img>
</div>

<Tip>
  Calibrations shift with every refresh, and the selection moves with them: the
  chain highlighted above was the best on an earlier snapshot than the one
  quoted in the code. Re-run `best_qubits` shortly before you submit.
</Tip>

## Running on the qubits you chose

### Rigetti direct: hand-placed native gates

On the [Rigetti direct path](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/rigetti),
programs that bypass quilc must already use
[native gates](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/rigetti#native-gates) on
physical qubits, which is exactly what the coupling map enables. A Bell pair
on the best-calibrated edge:

```python
import pyquil

q0, q1 = device.best_qubits(2)  # the run below used (88, 89)

program = pyquil.Program(f"""
DECLARE ro BIT[2]
RX(pi/2) {q0}
RX(pi/2) {q1}
CZ {q0} {q1}
RX(-pi/2) {q1}
MEASURE {q0} ro[0]
MEASURE {q1} ro[1]
""")

job = device.run(program, shots=100)
job.wait_for_final_state()
job.result().data.get_counts()
# {'00': 44, '11': 44, '01': 7, '10': 5}  -- run on Cepheus-1-108Q, 2026-07-21
```

The correlated outcomes (`00` and `11`) came back at 88 percent on hardware,
consistent with the roughly 0.4 percent CZ error and few-percent readout error
of the chosen pair.

<Note>
  This program contains no timing instruction, so it takes the **compiled**
  path. The placement survives because its qubits already fit the topology,
  which makes quilc default to identity (`NAIVE`) rewiring; quilc is not
  obligated to keep it in general. To make placement a guarantee rather than a
  default, add a clock-aligned delay to take the direct path, or pin the
  compiled path with `PRAGMA INITIAL_REWIRING "NAIVE"`. See [Pinning the
  circuit](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/rigetti#pinning-the-circuit).
</Note>

### Qiskit: constrain transpilation to the real topology

If you would rather let a transpiler do the routing, feed the coupling map to
Qiskit and pin your circuit to the chain you selected. This works for any
gate-model device on qBraid:

```python
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit.transpiler import CouplingMap

ghz = QuantumCircuit(5, 5)
ghz.h(0)
for i in range(4):
    ghz.cx(i, i + 1)
ghz.measure(range(5), range(5))

coupling = CouplingMap(
    [list(edge) for edge in garnet.coupling_map]
    + [[b, a] for a, b in garnet.coupling_map]
)
chain = list(garnet.best_qubits(5))  # [2, 7, 8, 13, 17] on Garnet, 2026-07-24

transpiled = transpile(
    ghz,
    coupling_map=coupling,
    initial_layout=chain,
    basis_gates=["r", "cz"],
    optimization_level=3,
)

job = garnet.run(transpiled, shots=1000)
```

Every two-qubit gate in the transpiled circuit now acts on a physically
coupled, well-calibrated pair, and no SWAP overhead is silently inserted for
qubits you did not choose.

<Warning>
  Transpile against the coupling map of the exact device ID you will submit to.
  Vendor-routed and direct device IDs share hardware and calibrations, but a
  circuit laid out for one device will not fit another.
</Warning>

# AQT
Source: https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/aqt

Run on Alpine Quantum Technologies' IBEX Q1 trapped-ion QPU through qBraid, with only a qBraid API key.

<Info>
  Using your own AQT arnica account? See [AQT
  (self-managed)](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/self-managed/aqt).
</Info>

## Devices on qBraid

[Alpine Quantum Technologies (AQT)](https://www.aqt.eu/)' IBEX Q1 is a 12-qubit trapped-ion QPU with all-to-all connectivity. It is on qBraid through two submission paths. Each path has its own device ID and billing.

| Device ID                    | Path                                                                      |
| :--------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `openquantum:aqt:qpu:ibex-q1` | [Open Quantum](#through-open-quantum)    |
| `aws:aqt:qpu:ibex-q1`        | [Amazon Braket](#through-amazon-braket) |

Check each device's status and price in the [device catalog](https://account.qbraid.com/devices) before you submit. Not every path is online at once.

## Quick start

```python
from qbraid.runtime import QbraidProvider

provider = QbraidProvider()
device = provider.get_device("aws:aqt:qpu:ibex-q1")

bell = """
OPENQASM 3.0;
include "stdgates.inc";
qubit[2] q;
bit[2] c;
h q[0];
cx q[0], q[1];
c = measure q;
"""

job = device.run(bell, shots=100)
print(job.result().data.get_counts())
```

Programs can be written in any framework qBraid supports.

## Through Amazon Braket

`aws:aqt:` devices go through Amazon Braket, billed in qBraid credits. Any two qubits can interact, so there is no coupling map to route around: [Calibrations](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/calibrations) returns an empty edge list for IBEX Q1. These devices take [Braket runtime options](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/aws#braket-runtime-options), and [Amazon Braket](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/aws) covers what every Braket device has in common, including how counts are ordered.

## Through Open Quantum

`openquantum:aqt:` devices go through Open Quantum and spend credits from an Open Quantum account linked to qBraid, not qBraid credits. Link the account first, then submit as usual:

```python
device = provider.get_device("openquantum:aqt:qpu:ibex-q1")
job = device.run(bell, shots=100)
```

See [Open Quantum](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/open-quantum) for linking an account and what these devices accept.

# GPU simulators
Source: https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/gpu-simulators

Running circuits on qBraid's GPU state-vector and tensor-network simulators through the QbraidProvider, with every option, their limits, daily allowance, and per-minute pricing.

<Info>
  Device IDs: `qbraid:qbraid:sim:gpu-sv` (state vector, up to 35 qubits) &nbsp;·&nbsp;
  `qbraid:qbraid:sim:gpu-tn` (tensor network, up to 500 qubits) &nbsp;·&nbsp; NVIDIA GH200
  &nbsp;·&nbsp; batch jobs &nbsp;·&nbsp; free daily allowance, then 5 credits per minute with
  usage-based billing &nbsp;·&nbsp; accessed through
  [`QbraidProvider`](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/getting-started)
</Info>

qBraid runs two GPU simulators on its Leo cluster, on NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper with 96 GB of
HBM3. They answer different questions:

| Simulator | Device ID                  | Use it for                                                                                                        |
| :-------- | :------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| gpu-sv    | `qbraid:qbraid:sim:gpu-sv` | **Exact** state-vector simulation of any circuit up to **35 qubits** (34 in double precision).                    |
| gpu-tn    | `qbraid:qbraid:sim:gpu-tn` | **Wide, low-entanglement** circuits, up to **500 qubits**, as a matrix product state (MPS) or exact contraction. |

If your circuit fits in 35 qubits, gpu-sv gives the exact answer whatever its entanglement. Past
that, gpu-tn can go much wider, as long as the circuit stays weakly entangled: GHZ states, shallow
circuits, and circuits whose two-qubit gates act on neighboring qubits.

<Note>
  Each GPU simulator has a **free daily allowance**: 25 circuits a day on Free, 125 on Standard,
  and unlimited on Pro and Enterprise. A single job is one circuit, and a batch counts one per
  circuit. Jobs past the allowance are refused unless you turn on
  usage-based billing, which charges them at 5 credits ($0.05) per minute. See
  [Pricing and daily allowance](#pricing-and-daily-allowance).
</Note>

## Quick start

Both simulators take OpenQASM 2 or OpenQASM 3. A Bell pair on gpu-sv:

```python
from qbraid.runtime import QbraidProvider

provider = QbraidProvider()
device = provider.get_device("qbraid:qbraid:sim:gpu-sv")

bell = """
OPENQASM 2.0;
include "qelib1.inc";
qreg q[2];
creg c[2];
h q[0];
cx q[0],q[1];
measure q -> c;
"""

job = device.run(bell, shots=1000)
print(job.result().data.get_counts())
# only '00' and '11', about half each: the simulation is exact and noiseless
```

A 100-qubit GHZ state is far past any state vector, but it is easy for gpu-tn. Writing it as a
chain of neighboring CNOTs keeps it fast:

```python
device = provider.get_device("qbraid:qbraid:sim:gpu-tn")

n = 100
lines = ["OPENQASM 2.0;", 'include "qelib1.inc";', f"qreg q[{n}];", f"creg c[{n}];", "h q[0];"]
lines += [f"cx q[{i}],q[{i + 1}];" for i in range(n - 1)]
lines.append("measure q -> c;")

job = device.run("\n".join(lines), shots=1000)
print(job.result().data.get_counts())
# only '000…0' and '111…1': a GHZ state stays exact under MPS at any width
```

## Runtime options

Device options go in the **`runtime_options`** dict, not in the `run()` signature. `shots` is the
exception: pass it to `run()` directly.

```python
job = device.run(program, shots=1000, runtime_options={"precision": "double"})
```

### gpu-sv

| Option      | Type | Default    | Effect                                                                                       |
| :---------- | :--- | :--------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `shots`     | int  | —          | 1 to **1,000,000**. Passed directly to `run()`, not in the dict.                             |
| `precision` | str  | `"single"` | `"single"` (complex64, up to **35** qubits) or `"double"` (complex128, up to **34** qubits). |
| `timeout`   | int  | none       | A time limit in whole seconds, at least 1. Checked between the steps of a job. See [Timeouts](#timeouts). |
| `seed`      | int  | none       | Seeds the sampling: the same seed, circuit and options return the same counts. 0 to 4,294,967,295 (2³² − 1). See [Reproducible counts](#reproducible-counts). |

Past 33 qubits in single precision, or 32 in double, the state vector is larger than the GPU's
memory, and gpu-sv keeps the rest in the GH200's host memory. That happens automatically, with no
option to set, and those jobs take longer: see [Execution time](#execution-time).

### gpu-tn

| Option            | Type  | Default    | Effect                                                                                                                                  |
| :---------------- | :---- | :--------- | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `shots`           | int   | —          | 1 to **10,000**. Passed directly to `run()`, not in the dict.                                                                           |
| `method`          | str   | `"mps"`    | `"mps"`: matrix product state, approximate once truncated. `"exact"`: full tensor-network contraction.                                 |
| `maxBondDim`      | int   | `64`       | MPS only. The largest bond dimension kept, 2 to 1024.                                                                                   |
| `relativeCutoff`  | float | `1e-5`     | MPS only. Singular values below this fraction of the largest are dropped. Strictly between 0 and 1.                                    |
| `absoluteCutoff`  | float | `1e-5`     | MPS only. Singular values below this value are dropped. Strictly between 0 and 1.                                                       |
| `precision`       | str   | `"double"` | `"double"` (complex128) or `"single"` (complex64).                                                                                      |
| `numHyperSamples` | int   | 8          | `exact` only. The number of hyper-samples the contraction-path finder tries, at least 1. Accepted and ignored for `mps`.                 |
| `timeout`         | int   | none       | A time limit in whole seconds, at least 1. Sampling is stopped when it runs out. See [Timeouts](#timeouts).                            |
| `svdAlgorithm`    | str   | `"GESVDJ"` | MPS only. The SVD that truncates the bonds: `"GESVD"` (QR), `"GESVDJ"` (Jacobi) or `"GESVDP"` (polar decomposition). Accepted and ignored for `exact`. |
| `seed`            | int   | none       | Seeds the sampling, with either method. 0 to 4,294,967,295 (2³² − 1). See [Reproducible counts](#reproducible-counts).               |

```python
device = provider.get_device("qbraid:qbraid:sim:gpu-tn")

job = device.run(program, shots=1000, runtime_options={"maxBondDim": 256, "relativeCutoff": 1e-8})
job = device.run(program, shots=1000, runtime_options={"method": "exact"})
```

Both simulators also accept `irType` (`"qasm2"` or `"qasm3"`). It only labels the input: the
program's own `OPENQASM` header selects the parser, so you don't need to set it.

<Warning>
  **The two simulators default to different precisions.** gpu-sv defaults to `"single"`, which is
  what reaches 35 qubits; gpu-tn defaults to `"double"`.
</Warning>

### Reproducible counts

Pass a `seed` and the same circuit, options and seed return the same counts:

```python
job = device.run(program, shots=1000, runtime_options={"seed": 42})
```

Leave it out and each run draws a fresh sample. Counts are reproducible on the same simulator
release; a later release may sample differently from the same seed.

### What is not an option

- **The MPS gauge.** On gpu-tn, `maxBondDim`, the two cutoffs and `svdAlgorithm` are the only
  controls over MPS truncation.

### How a bad option is refused

Options are checked when the job runs. An option the simulator doesn't know, or a value out of
range, fails the job: it ends `FAILED`, is charged 0 credits, and its status message names the
option.

```python
job = device.run(program, shots=1000, runtime_options={"max_bond_dim": 128})
job.wait_for_final_state()
print(job.status().status_message)
# Unknown option 'max_bond_dim'
```

The messages take two forms:

```text
Unknown option '<name>'
Invalid option '<name>': <what the value must be>
```

For example:

```text
Unknown option 'gauge'
Invalid option 'maxBondDim': must be less than or equal to 1024
Invalid option 'relativeCutoff': must be greater than 0
Invalid option 'numHyperSamples': must be greater than or equal to 1
Invalid option 'precision': must be 'single' or 'double'
```

## Choosing an MPS or exact contraction on gpu-tn

### MPS is approximate once bonds are truncated

A matrix product state is exact while every bond stays within `maxBondDim`. Highly entangling
circuits, such as deep random circuits or a QFT on a wide register, need larger bonds. Past
`maxBondDim`, or below the cutoffs, the simulator truncates, and the counts are sampled from an
approximation. GHZ and other low-entanglement circuits stay exact at any width.

### Choosing maxBondDim and the cutoffs

The defaults, `maxBondDim` 64 and both cutoffs at `1e-5`, keep many circuits exact. Setting them
too low shows up in the counts. On a 16-qubit mirror circuit, 12 random `u3` and `cx` brickwork
layers followed by their inverse, the ideal outcome is all zeros with probability 1. With 1,000
shots:

| Options                                       | Share of shots on all zeros | Distinct outcomes |
| :-------------------------------------------- | --------------------------: | ----------------: |
| defaults (`maxBondDim` 64)                     |                       1.000 |                 1 |
| `maxBondDim` 2                                 |                       0.012 |               676 |
| `maxBondDim` 4                                 |                       0.153 |               519 |
| `relativeCutoff` 0.2 and `absoluteCutoff` 0.2 |                       0.843 |                54 |
| `method` `"exact"`                            |                       1.000 |                 1 |
| `precision` `"single"`                        |                       1.000 |                 1 |

To check whether truncation matters for your circuit, run it again with a larger `maxBondDim`, or
with `method: "exact"` if the circuit is small, and compare the counts. If they agree, the smaller
setting was enough.

Raising `maxBondDim` costs memory and time. Time grows roughly with the cube of the bond
dimension: a 64-qubit random circuit of depth 30 took about 7 s at `maxBondDim` 64 and about 30 s
at 256. To truncate less without raising `maxBondDim`, lower the cutoffs. Both must stay above 0,
so send a tiny value such as `1e-12` rather than 0.

### MPS runs one- and two-qubit gates

With `mps`, every gate on three or more qubits is rewritten into exactly equivalent one- and
two-qubit gates before it runs. This adds gates: a Toffoli becomes 8, and an X with four controls
becomes 88. A gate with more than 6 controls is refused under `mps`:

```text
Method 'mps' runs gates with at most 6 control qubits (a controlled swap counts one more, for its
second target); this circuit has a gate with 7. Use method 'exact' for it.
```

`exact` runs those gates as written.

### Exact contraction: an estimate, then a 10-minute stop

Exact contraction can take far longer than MPS, and its cost climbs steeply with width and depth.
Two protections keep an `exact` job from holding the GPU indefinitely.

1. **An up-front estimate.** Before an `exact` job contracts anything, gpu-tn estimates its cost
   and refuses a circuit estimated beyond what the GPU can sample within the job's time limit:

   ```text
   Exact tensor-network contraction of this circuit is estimated at … floating-point operations,
   beyond what the GPU can sample within the job's time limit. Use method 'mps' (the default) or a
   smaller circuit.
   ```

2. **The 10-minute stop.** The estimate catches many out-of-reach circuits, but not all. A job it
   lets through is still stopped after [10 minutes](#timeouts). A 32-qubit QFT followed by its
   inverse passed the estimate under `exact`, ran for 10 minutes, and was stopped with
   `Exact tensor-network contraction exceeded 10 minutes and was stopped. Use method 'mps' (the
   default) or a smaller circuit.` The stopped job failed and was charged 0 credits. The same
   circuit took 10.6 s under `mps`.

## Timeouts

`timeout` is a whole number of seconds, at least 1. `0` is refused; it does not mean "no limit".
Leave the option out for no per-request limit.

**gpu-tn** samples every job in a separate process that is stopped after **10 minutes**, or when
your `timeout` runs out if that comes first. The message says which limit stopped it:

```text
Matrix product state simulation exceeded the request's timeout of 30 seconds and was stopped.
Exact tensor-network contraction exceeded the request's timeout of 30 seconds and was stopped.
Matrix product state simulation exceeded 10 minutes and was stopped. Use a smaller maxBondDim, fewer shots or a smaller circuit.
Exact tensor-network contraction exceeded 10 minutes and was stopped. Use method 'mps' (the default) or a smaller circuit.
```

A job that finishes in time keeps its result. A stopped job fails and is not charged.

**gpu-sv** checks `timeout` between the steps of a job, not during the GPU simulation itself, so a
simulation that is already running can take longer than the limit. A job stopped by it fails with:

```text
Simulation exceeded the allowed time limit of 30 seconds.
```

gpu-tn reports the same message when its `timeout` runs out before sampling has started.

## What a circuit may contain

Both simulators accept the same programs.

- **OpenQASM 2 and OpenQASM 3.** The program's own `OPENQASM` header selects the parser. Loops,
  custom gates, subroutines, broadcasts, and aliases are unrolled before the circuit runs.
- **Every gate of `qelib1.inc` and `stdgates.inc`**, plus the `ctrl @`, `negctrl @`, `inv @`, and
  integer `pow @` modifiers.
- **Hardware qubits** (`$0`, `$1`, …), as `qiskit.qasm3.dumps` writes a transpiled circuit. `$3` is
  qubit 3. A program cannot mix them with declared qubits.
- **`barrier` and `delay`** are accepted and ignored.

Circuits measure at the end. These are refused with a message that names the feature, such as
`Unsupported OpenQASM feature: mid-circuit measurement ('h' acts on q[0] after it was measured)`:

- a gate on a qubit after it was measured (mid-circuit measurement)
- `reset` after a gate or measurement on that qubit. A `reset` of a qubit nothing has acted on yet is
  skipped, since the qubit is still in |0⟩.
- `while` loops, and classical control flow on measured bits (`if`, `switch`)
- assigning or initializing classical bits other than by measurement
- `pragma`, `box`, pulse-level `cal` and `defcal`, and `input` or `output` declarations
- gates with no definition (`opaque`) and non-integer `pow @`

## Reading the results

Count keys follow your circuit's classical register, with **classical bit 0 rightmost**, the same
convention as Qiskit and every qBraid simulator. Classical bits that no measurement writes read
`0`. Multiple registers are concatenated in declaration order, with the last register leftmost.

A circuit with no measurements reports every qubit, with qubit 0 rightmost.

Each result also records how the job was simulated. The fields are in the result's `details`:

```python
result = job.result()
print(result.data.get_counts())
print(result.details["simulationMethod"], result.details["precision"])
```

| Field                                              | gpu-sv          | gpu-tn                                                         |
| :------------------------------------------------- | :-------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `numQubits`                                        | Circuit width   | Circuit width                                                  |
| `precision`                                        | The precision used | The precision used                                         |
| `simulationMethod`                                 | `"statevector"` | `"matrix_product_state"` (`mps`) or `"tensor_network"` (`exact`) |
| `maxBondDim`, `relativeCutoff`, `absoluteCutoff`   | Not present     | `mps` only: the truncation settings the counts were sampled under |

So an MPS result always carries the approximation it was sampled under. Exact results omit the
MPS fields.

## Batch jobs

Both GPU simulators support [batch jobs](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/jobs#batch-jobs)
(`device.profile.batch_job_support` is `True`). Pass a list of circuits with `as_batch=True` and
they run as **one job**, with one job ID and one status, and you get one set of counts per circuit,
in order:

```python
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit

bell = QuantumCircuit(2)
bell.h(0)
bell.cx(0, 1)
bell.measure_all()

ghz = QuantumCircuit(3)
ghz.h(0)
ghz.cx(0, 1)
ghz.cx(1, 2)
ghz.measure_all()

job = device.run([bell, ghz], shots=200, as_batch=True)
job.result().data.get_counts()
# [{'00': 99, '11': 101}, {'000': 108, '111': 92}]
```

The circuits run one after another in the same GPU allocation, so a batch skips the submission and
queueing overhead that separate jobs each pay.

- **The daily allowance counts circuits.** A batch of N circuits uses N of the day's free circuits.
  See [Pricing and daily allowance](#pricing-and-daily-allowance).
- **One set of options for the whole batch.** `runtime_options` apply to every circuit in it.
- **Circuits fail on their own.** One circuit that fails, for example on an unsupported gate,
  doesn't fail the others. Each failed circuit's result says why.
- **The time limit covers the whole batch.** A circuit that couldn't finish before the job's time
  limit isn't started, and its result says to submit it again in a new job:

  ```text
  Not run: the batch reached its time limit before this circuit could start. Submit it again in a new job.
  ```

Without `as_batch=True`, a list of circuits is submitted as **separate jobs**, one per circuit,
and `run()` returns a list of jobs.

## Pricing and daily allowance

Each GPU simulator has its own **free daily allowance** of circuits. A single job is one circuit,
and a [batch](#batch-jobs) of N circuits is N. A job counts against the allowance when you submit
it, and the count resets at **00:00 UTC**.

| Plan       | Free circuits per day, per GPU simulator |
| :--------- | ---------------------------------------: |
| Free       |                                       25 |
| Standard   |                                      125 |
| Pro        |                                Unlimited |
| Enterprise |                                Unlimited |

- **Jobs inside the allowance are free.** The simulator's price is waived.
- **A job inside the allowance that fails or is cancelled** gives its place in the allowance back.
  A batch that fails part-way keeps the places of the circuits that completed and gives back the
  rest.
- **Once the allowance is used**, further jobs are refused until the next reset:

  ```text
  Daily free allowance for qbraid:qbraid:sim:gpu-sv reached (25/day). Resets at midnight UTC.
  Enable usage-based billing for simulators to keep running jobs, charged from your credits at the
  device's per-minute price.
  ```

  A batch is admitted whole or not at all. One bigger than what remains of the allowance is refused
  before it runs:

  ```text
  This batch of 30 circuits needs 30 slots of your daily free allowance for qbraid:qbraid:sim:gpu-sv,
  and 23 of 25 remain today. Resets at midnight UTC. Submit fewer circuits, or enable usage-based
  billing for simulators to run the whole batch, charged from your credits at the device's
  per-minute price.
  ```

- **With usage-based billing turned on**, those further jobs run and are charged from your credits
  at **5 credits per minute** ($0.05), in proportion to each job's execution time, with a minimum of
  **3 seconds** (0.25 credits) per single-circuit job. A batch that doesn't fit in the allowance
  runs paid as a whole.
- **A job that fails is not charged**, inside or beyond the allowance. That includes a job refused
  for a bad option and a job stopped at a time limit. A batch where some circuits fail is charged
  for its full execution time; one where none complete is free.

| Execution time | Credits charged            |
| :------------- | :------------------------- |
| 1.0 s          | 0.25, the 3-second minimum |
| 14.3 s         | about 1.19                 |
| 21.8 s         | about 1.82                 |

Usage-based billing is off unless you turn it on. Turn it on with **Usage-based billing for GPU
simulators** on the **Simulator Usage** card in **Account > Usage**. See
[Simulator usage](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/account/usage#simulator-usage). Pro and Enterprise plans have no daily limit,
so they never need it.

## Execution time

These are the execution times that jobs recorded on the GH200 at simulator version 0.3.1, with
1,000 shots. Execution time is what usage-based billing charges for. Your circuits will differ, but
the shape holds. The circuits are:

- **GHZ, fan-out**: H on qubit 0, then a CNOT from qubit 0 to every other qubit.
- **Random brickwork, depth d**: d layers, each a random `u3` on every qubit and CNOTs on
  alternating neighboring pairs.
- **Mirror brickwork, depth d**: the same brickwork followed by its inverse.
- **QFT and inverse**: a QFT followed by its inverse, which has controlled phases between every pair
  of qubits.

**gpu-sv**, single precision unless marked:

| Circuit                            | 30 qubits | 31 qubits | 32 qubits | 33 qubits |
| :--------------------------------- | --------: | --------: | --------: | --------: |
| GHZ, fan-out                       |     1.1 s |     1.2 s |     1.3 s |     1.6 s |
| QFT and inverse                    |     1.4 s |     1.7 s |     2.2 s |     3.3 s |
| Random brickwork, depth 10         |     1.3 s |     1.5 s |     1.9 s |     2.8 s |
| Random brickwork, depth 50         |     1.9 s |     2.8 s |     4.5 s |     7.9 s |
| Mirror brickwork, depth 50         |     2.7 s |     4.3 s |     7.6 s |    14.3 s |
| Random brickwork, depth 50, double |     2.1 s |     3.1 s |     5.3 s |         — |

In the same measurements, every gpu-sv job up to 28 qubits, in either precision and for every
circuit above, recorded under 1.6 s, so it would be charged the 3-second minimum.

Past 33 qubits in single precision, or 32 in double, part of the state vector is in host memory,
and each added qubit costs more than double. Measured at simulator version 0.4.0 on the same GPU,
with 1,000 shots:

| Circuit                    | 34 qubits, single | 35 qubits, single | 33 qubits, double | 34 qubits, double |
| :------------------------- | ----------------: | ----------------: | ----------------: | ----------------: |
| GHZ, fan-out               |             4.8 s |            10.6 s |             4.7 s |            10.5 s |
| QFT and inverse            |            10.8 s |            23.7 s |             9.5 s |            21.1 s |
| Random brickwork, depth 10 |             7.4 s |            15.9 s |             6.2 s |            13.7 s |
| Random brickwork, depth 50 |            19.0 s |            42.2 s |            13.4 s |            28.4 s |
| Mirror brickwork, depth 50 |            34.9 s |            74.6 s |            22.0 s |            46.5 s |

**gpu-tn** with `mps` and the default settings:

| Circuit                    | 64 qubits | 128 qubits | 256 qubits | 500 qubits |
| :------------------------- | --------: | ---------: | ---------: | ---------: |
| GHZ, fan-out               |     3.1 s |      7.9 s |     26.8 s |     97.3 s |
| Mirror brickwork, depth 10 |     2.7 s |      4.0 s |      6.6 s |     11.5 s |
| Random brickwork, depth 10 |     2.2 s |      3.0 s |      4.4 s |      7.3 s |
| Random brickwork, depth 50 |    10.8 s |     21.8 s |     43.9 s |     85.6 s |

The QFT and inverse, with its long-range gates, took 10.6 s at 32 qubits, 74.9 s at 64, and
281.7 s at 100.

**gpu-tn** with `method: "exact"`:

| Circuit                    | 8 qubits | 16 qubits | 24 qubits |                     32 qubits |
| :------------------------- | -------: | --------: | --------: | ----------------------------: |
| GHZ, fan-out               |    2.5 s |     2.6 s |     2.7 s |                         3.5 s |
| Mirror brickwork, depth 10 |    3.0 s |     3.4 s |     5.2 s |                         197 s |
| QFT and inverse            |    8.4 s |    21.8 s |    24.7 s | stopped at 10 minutes, 0 credits |

<Tip>
  **On gpu-tn, gate locality matters more than width.** MPS applies a two-qubit gate between
  distant qubits through a chain of swaps. The same 500-qubit GHZ state took about 3 s as a
  nearest-neighbor chain and about 97 s as a fan-out from qubit 0. Lay out circuits so that
  qubits that interact are adjacent. Sampling cost also grows with shots × width, so wide
  circuits stay slow even when they are easy to represent.
</Tip>

## Troubleshooting

A job that fails reports the reason as its status message: `job.status().status_message`.

| Symptom                                                                                                                  | Cause                                                                                                                                            |
| :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Unknown option '<name>'`, for example `Unknown option 'max_bond_dim'`                        | The simulator has no option by that name. Check the spelling against [Runtime options](#runtime-options).     |
| `Invalid option '<name>': …`, for example `Invalid option 'maxBondDim': must be less than or equal to 1024`              | The value is out of range or the wrong type. The message says what it must be.                                                                   |
| `Number of qubits in the circuit (36) exceeds the device's capacity (35).`                                               | The SDK refuses the job before it is submitted: gpu-sv's limit is 35 qubits.                                                                     |
| `… Circuit has 35 qubits, exceeding the maximum of 34 that this environment's GPU nodes simulate at this precision. Use fewer qubits.` | Double precision tops out at 34 qubits on gpu-sv. Use `"single"`, the default, which reaches 35. The job is not charged.          |
| `Not enough free GPU memory: a …-qubit …-precision state vector needs … MiB, but … MiB is free. Retry later, or use fewer qubits.` | gpu-sv checks free GPU memory before it allocates the state vector. Retry later, or use fewer qubits.                      |
| `Not enough free host memory on this node: a 35-qubit single-precision state vector extends beyond the GPU only while the node has 291272 MiB of memory available, and it has … MiB. …` | Past 33 qubits single (32 double), part of the state vector goes in host memory, and the node has too little free right now. Retry later, or use fewer qubits. |
| `Circuit has 501 qubits, exceeding the maximum of 500 for tensor network simulation`                                     | gpu-tn's hard limit is 500 qubits.                                                                                                               |
| gpu-tn counts don't match the exact distribution                                                                         | MPS is approximate once a bond exceeds `maxBondDim`. See [Choosing maxBondDim and the cutoffs](#choosing-maxbonddim-and-the-cutoffs).            |
| `Exact tensor-network contraction of this circuit is estimated at …`                                                     | The `exact` estimate refused the circuit. Use `mps` or a smaller circuit.                                                                        |
| `… exceeded 10 minutes and was stopped.`                                                                                 | gpu-tn's 10-minute limit. The job is not charged. See [Timeouts](#timeouts).                                                                     |
| `Method 'mps' runs gates with at most 6 control qubits …`                                                                | Use `method: "exact"` for gates with more than 6 controls.                                                                                       |
| `Unsupported OpenQASM feature: …`                                                                                        | The circuit uses a feature these simulators refuse. See [What a circuit may contain](#what-a-circuit-may-contain).                               |
| `Daily free allowance for … reached`                                                                                     | You have used today's free circuits on that simulator. Wait for 00:00 UTC, or turn on [usage-based billing](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/account/usage#simulator-usage).   |

# IonQ
Source: https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/ionq

Run on IonQ's Forte trapped-ion QPUs and the IonQ simulator through qBraid, with only a qBraid API key.

<Info>
  Using your own IonQ API key? See [IonQ
  (self-managed)](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/self-managed/ionq).
</Info>

## Devices on qBraid

IonQ's trapped-ion systems are on qBraid through three submission paths. Each path has its own device IDs, billing, and runtime options.

| Device ID                               | Device                    | Path                                    |
| :-------------------------------------- | :------------------------ | :-------------------------------------- |
| `ionq:ionq:sim:simulator`               | IonQ simulator, 29 qubits | [Direct](#direct)                       |
| `ionq:ionq:qpu:forte-1`                 | Forte-1, 36 qubits        | [Direct](#direct)                       |
| `aws:ionq:qpu:forte-1`                  | Forte-1, 36 qubits        | [Amazon Braket](#through-amazon-braket) |
| `aws:ionq:qpu:forte-enterprise-1`       | Forte Enterprise-1        | [Amazon Braket](#through-amazon-braket) |
| `openquantum:ionq:qpu:forte-1`          | Forte-1, 36 qubits        | [Open Quantum](#through-open-quantum)   |
| `openquantum:ionq:qpu:forte-enterprise` | Forte Enterprise          | [Open Quantum](#through-open-quantum)   |

Check each device's status and price in the [device catalog](https://account.qbraid.com/devices) before you submit. Not every path is online at once.

## Quick start

Start on the simulator, which runs the same programs as the QPUs:

```python
from qbraid.runtime import QbraidProvider

provider = QbraidProvider()
device = provider.get_device("ionq:ionq:sim:simulator")

bell = """
OPENQASM 3.0;
include "stdgates.inc";
qubit[2] q;
bit[2] c;
h q[0];
cx q[0], q[1];
c = measure q;
"""

job = device.run(bell, shots=100)
print(job.result().data.get_counts())
```

To run on a QPU, change the device ID. Programs can be written in any framework qBraid supports; qBraid converts them to OpenQASM before they reach IonQ.

## Direct

`ionq:` devices go from qBraid straight to IonQ, billed in qBraid credits. They accept these `runtime_options`, which qBraid passes to IonQ unchanged:

| Option             | Effect                                                                 |
| :----------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `noise`            | On the simulator, a hardware noise model and optional seed. See below. |
| `error_mitigation` | IonQ's error mitigation settings, such as debiasing, on QPU jobs.      |
| `metadata`         | Key-value metadata stored with the IonQ job.                           |

Run the simulator with a hardware noise profile:

```python
job = device.run(
    bell,
    shots=1000,
    runtime_options={"noise": {"model": "aria-1", "seed": 42}},
)
```

Noise models include `ideal`, `harmony`, `harmony-1`, `harmony-2`, `aria-1`, `aria-2`, `forte-1` and `forte-enterprise-1`. See IonQ's guide to [simulation with noise models](https://docs.ionq.com/guides/simulation-with-noise-models).

## Through Amazon Braket

`aws:ionq:` devices go through Amazon Braket, billed in qBraid credits. They take [Braket runtime options](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/aws#braket-runtime-options) rather than the direct options above. Debiasing, for example, is set with `device_parameters`:

```python
device = provider.get_device("aws:ionq:qpu:forte-1")

job = device.run(
    bell,
    shots=2500,  # Braket requires at least 2500 shots for debiasing
    runtime_options={"device_parameters": {"errorMitigation": "Debias"}},
)
```

[Amazon Braket](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/aws) covers what every Braket device has in common, including how counts are ordered.

## Through Open Quantum

`openquantum:ionq:` devices go through Open Quantum and spend credits from an Open Quantum account linked to qBraid, not qBraid credits. Link the account first, then submit as usual:

```python
device = provider.get_device("openquantum:ionq:qpu:forte-1")
job = device.run(bell, shots=100)
```

See [Open Quantum](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/open-quantum) for linking an account and what these devices accept.

## Related links

- [Run on qBraid](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/getting-started): installing the SDK and saving your qBraid API key
- [Batch & group jobs](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/jobs): running several circuits as separate, batch, or group jobs
- [IonQ (self-managed)](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/self-managed/ionq): `IonQProvider` with your own IonQ API key, including IonQ's native gates
- [IonQ documentation](https://docs.ionq.com/)

[Amazon Braket](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/aws#how-braket-compiles-your-circuit) explains the compilation, how your counts are ordered, and how to retrieve the compiled program to see which physical qubits your job ran on.

Garnet and Emerald report live calibration data through qBraid. [Calibrations](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/calibrations) shows how to fetch it, plot the connectivity graph, and pick the best qubits for your circuit.

`aws:iqm:` devices take [Braket runtime options](https://docs.qbraid.com/v2/sdk/user-guide/providers/aws#braket-runtime-options). For example, IQM's dynamic circuits, with mid-circuit measurement, are a Braket experimental capability:

job = device.run(

)
